text.p: U.S. grain prices rose briskly on Thursday on forecasts for bitter cold weather in the US Plains and concerns of "winter kill" for the crops.
Harsh spring weather in several key wheat growing regions of the U.S. boosted CBOT soft red winter wheat futures to a strongly higher close, traders said.

The concerns for wheat stretched from the spring wheat belt to the hard red winter growing states of the U.S. Plains. Wheat closed 7-1/2 to nine cents per bushel higher, with May up 7-1/2 at $3.93 a bushel.

Wheat was further supported by forecasts for up to 10 inches of snow in key spring wheat planting areas. Farmers must wait for a massive snowpack to melt and soil to dry enough before they begin seeding spring wheat, traders said.

Base metal trading was mostly low-key on the LME on Thursday, with prices gradually crumbling towards softer closes, traders said. Copper and aluminium held up relatively well, with losses from Wednesday restricted to single figures, but the other metals came in for moderate speculative selling, they said.
Late losses in metals such as zinc, lead, tin and nickel reflected disappointed liquidation after earlier failures at overhead resistance levels.

Copper had managed to hold above the $2,300 a tonne level, but given the lack of resolve overhead -- resistance is strong between $2,310 and $2,320 -- the market looked set to test the downside again, traders said. Last three months business was at $2,302, down just $5 from Wednesday. The cash/threes backwardation eased modestly to $45/47.
Aluminium was unable to clear $1,600, despite an LME stock fall and a drop in February IPAI producer inventories. Prices ended the kerb at $1,586, down $6.
Nickel moved lower from early levels above $7,500. Last trade was at $7,375, a $115 loss.

Lead and zinc stalled at respective resistance levels in the mid-$650s and mid-$1,260s, but declines were largely confined to the kerb. Lead ended $12 lower at $639, while zinc finished $22 softer at $1,244.
Tin followed the overall trend, and closed $70 down at $5,690. However, the alloy market was stable at $1,470/75 a tonne.

New York precious metals recovered from some early weakness to end higher Thursday, with the exception of palladium which gave back Wednesday's gains after news Russia may resume exports to Japan in May. COMEX June gold ended up 50 cents at $351.00 an ounce, with support still seen around $350 and resistance around $352.00, within the $348.30-358.00 range of the past month. In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted $348.40/90, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $347.60 and the New York close Wednesday around $347.80/30.

Crude oil was under pressure in a market that began to take a less rosy view of upcoming US gasoline demand. North Sea Brent Blend crude futures, a world benchmark, for May were trading around $17.70 per barrel late in London's day, down almost 50 cents from Wednesday afternoon.

However, NYMEX crude futures jumped sharply Thursday afternoon, mainly on technical factors. May crude closed up 30 cents at $19.57 a barrel. Traders said some market support came from an escalating dispute between Germany, the European Union and Iran after a German court found Iran had ordered the execution of Kurd dissidents in 1992; also, from the temporary closure of the Houston Ship Channel after a barge capsized there.
